The [Lockheed Martin X-35][ref_x35] won, which makes it the only aircraft in this series so far whose
demonstrator became a production programme, and it won partly on one flight. On 20 July 2001 the
[X-35B][ref_x35b] took off in a few hundred feet, climbed to twenty-five thousand feet, accelerated past the
speed of sound in level flight, returned to the field and landed vertically.
**No aircraft had ever done those three things in one sortie, the rival demonstrator could not, and the [contract followed three months later][ref_lm_award].**
This is the thirty-sixth article in the [X-Planes series][related_post_a297_xplanes_framing], following the
[X-1][related_post_a298_bell_x1], the [X-2][related_post_a299_bell_x2], the

**That sortie is called [Mission X][ref_missionx] and it is the most famous single flight any aircraft in this series ever made.**
It is also the reason this article exists, because a flight that famous invites exactly one question and the
question has a real answer. **What did it establish?**

## The Research Question

### The Sortie Has a Reputation and the Reputation Is Doing Work

The short version, repeated in almost every account, is that the X-35B did in one flight what the
[X-32][related_post_a329_boeing_x32] could not do at all, that the rival had to be physically reconfigured
between the hovering and supersonic parts of its envelope, and that the fly-off was therefore decided by a
capability one team had and the other did not.

**Every clause of that is true and the conclusion still does not follow from it, because the flight was not the experiment.**
A demonstration that three regimes can be flown in sequence is a demonstration about sequencing. Whether
sequencing was the hard part is a separate question, and it is one nobody asks, because the answer feels
obvious and is not.

### What This Article Will Not Do

**The previous article on the losing side of this competition already made the argument that neither demonstrator was the aircraft being bought**,
and made it at length. The X-32 and the X-35 were concept demonstrators, the F-32 and the F-35 were the
products, and the machines that flew in 2000 and 2001 differed from the machines under contract in
structure, in systems, in weight and in purpose.
**That is a construct-validity argument, it is correct, and it is made. It will not be remade here.**

What is left over is the winner's question, and it is a different one. Granting that the demonstrator was a
demonstrator, **what did its most celebrated flight actually demonstrate?**

### The Question, Stated So That It Can Be Answered Wrongly

A sortie that performs three manoeuvres in sequence tests something the same three manoeuvres flown on three
separate days do not, **if and only if the three place demands on the same hardware that interfere.** If
they do interfere, sequencing them is an existence proof and the flight is evidence. If they do not,
sequencing them is scheduling and the flight is a display.

**So the keystone of this article is a coupling question, and it is answerable.** For each of the three
events, and for the transitions between them, the article asks what physical quantity was actually scarce,
and computes it. The answer is not the one the reputation implies, and the article's own counter-arguments
against that answer are set out in a later section rather than suppressed.

**A preview, because a reader is entitled to know where an argument is going.** Two of the three events turn
out to have been cheap, one of them very cheap indeed, and the expensive thing is not one of the three.
**It is the conversion between modes, which is not in the name of the trick.** Worse for the reputation, and
this is the fact the whole argument turns on,
**the first in-flight conversion had already been flown eleven days earlier, on a sortie that also went faster than Mission X did.**

## Programme Origin

### What Was Being Bought

The [Joint Strike Fighter programme][ref_jsf] sought a single airframe family for three services and two
navies, with a conventional variant, a carrier variant and a [short-takeoff and vertical-landing][ref_stovl]
variant sharing enough structure and systems to be affordable.
**The short-takeoff and vertical-landing requirement is the one that constrains everything**, because it
demands that an aircraft otherwise sized for supersonic combat also hover, and hovering is the most
thrust-hungry thing an aeroplane can do.

The competition ran as a fly-off between two concept demonstrator teams. Each built and flew aircraft
covering the three variants, and each demonstrated a different answer to the hovering problem.

### The Invention

The X-35's answer is due to [Paul Bevilaqua][ref_bevilaqua] and Paul Shumpert at the Lockheed Skunk Works,
patented in 1993, and it is a genuinely unusual idea.
**Instead of pointing the engine's own exhaust downward, take mechanical power off the engine's shaft, run it forward through a clutch and a bevel gearbox, and use it to drive a separate fan that blows cold air straight down.**

Almost every reader's first reaction is that this is a worse deal, because the fan's thrust has to come out
of the engine's thrust and a shaft cannot create energy.
**The reaction is correct about the energy and wrong about the thrust, and the reason is the single most important relation in this article.**

### The Three Aircraft

Two airframes were built. The X-35A flew first, in the conventional configuration, and was then rebuilt as
the X-35B by installing the lift system. The X-35C was a separate aircraft with the larger wing and the
structure of the carrier variant.
**So the aircraft that flew Mission X is the same airframe that had earlier flown as a conventional fighter**,
which matters later, because it means the conventional and hovering configurations differed by an
installation rather than by an airframe.

## Sizing From First Principles

### The Relation That Makes a Fan Worth Carrying

**The previous article on the X-32 derived this and it is reused rather than rebuilt.** A jet that
accelerates a mass flow $\dot{m}$ from rest to a velocity $v$ produces a thrust and carries away a kinetic
power,

$$T = \dot{m} v \qquad \text{and} \qquad P = \tfrac{1}{2} \dot{m} v^{2}$$

and eliminating the velocity between them gives the relation that governs every lift system ever built,

$$T = \sqrt{2 P \dot{m}}$$

**At a fixed power, thrust rises as the square root of the mass flow.** The identity was tested over twenty
thousand randomised combinations of mass flow and jet velocity without a failure.

The consequence is the whole argument for a lift fan. A shaft cannot create power, so the fan's power does
come out of the engine. **But the fan moves air that the engine never touched**, and adding mass flow at
fixed power buys thrust. Doubling the mass flow multiplies the thrust by the square root of two even though
not one extra joule was spent.

**Said the other way round, and this is the form that makes the design decision obvious, thrust per unit power is inversely proportional to jet velocity**,
since $T/P = 2/v$. A hovering aeroplane wants the slowest, fattest jet it can arrange. A supersonic
aeroplane wants the opposite.
**The lift fan exists because those two wants are irreconcilable in one nozzle and reconcilable in two.**

### The Fan as an Actuator Disc

**Three published numbers fix the fan completely and none of them was published in order to.** The
[Rolls-Royce LiftFan][ref_liftfan] is fifty inches in diameter, produces twenty thousand pounds force of
thrust, and absorbs twenty-nine thousand shaft horsepower.

Writing $D$ for the diameter, the disc area is

$$A = \frac{\pi D^{2}}{4} = \frac{\pi \times 1.27^{2}}{4} = 1.2668 \ \text{m}^{2}$$

[Momentum theory][ref_momentum] treats the fan as a disc across which pressure jumps, with air arriving at
rest and leaving at a velocity that is twice the velocity through the disc itself. Writing $v_i$ for the
induced velocity at the disc and $\rho$ for sea-level density, thrust and mass flow give

$$T = 2 \rho A v_i^{2} \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad v_i = \sqrt{\frac{T}{2 \rho A}}$$

and substituting twenty thousand pounds force, which is 88,964 newtons,

$$v_i = \sqrt{\frac{88{,}964}{2 \times 1.225 \times 1.2668}} = 169.3 \ \text{m/s}$$

so the fully developed jet runs at 338.6 metres per second and the mass flow through the disc is

$$\dot{m} = \rho A v_i = 1.225 \times 1.2668 \times 169.3 = 262.7 \ \text{kg/s}$$

**which is 579.2 pounds per second, and that number deserves a pause.** It is roughly twice the entire
airflow of the engine driving it. **The fan is not an accessory. It is the larger air handler of the two.**

The ideal power such a disc requires is the thrust times the induced velocity,

$$P_{\text{ideal}} = T v_i = 88{,}964 \times 169.3 = 15.06 \ \text{MW}$$

against the 21.63 megawatts that twenty-nine thousand shaft horsepower actually delivers, so the fan's
figure of merit is

$$\mathrm{FM} = \frac{P_{\text{ideal}}}{P_{\text{shaft}}} = \frac{15.06}{21.63} = 0.697$$

**This is the same 0.697 the previous article recovered while examining the rival**, from the same three
numbers, and it is worth saying plainly that it belongs to the X-35's fan rather than the X-32's. A figure
of merit near seven tenths is respectable for a heavily loaded fan in a short duct with louvred exit vanes
and no time to be elegant.

The result was reached here by a route the earlier derivation did not use. Rather than evaluating the closed
form for induced velocity, the far-field velocity was recovered by bisecting the streamtube mass balance,
and the power was then taken as the jet's kinetic flux rather than as thrust times induced velocity.
**The two routes agree to the last bit of double precision, and it is worth being clear about what that does and does not establish.**
The formulations are algebraically equivalent, so exact agreement is what they ought to produce and is no
evidence that the physics is right. **What the second route tests is transcription**, and a mistyped
exponent or a dropped factor of two would break it immediately.

### What the Whole System Multiplies

The lift system's three contributors are the fan at twenty thousand pounds force, the three-bearing swivel
module at eighteen thousand, and two roll posts at 1,950 pounds force each, giving

$$T_{\text{total}} = 20{,}000 + 18{,}000 + 2 \times 1{,}950 = 41{,}900 \ \text{lbf}$$

**against an [engine][ref_f119] whose dry thrust is twenty-five thousand pounds force.** A direct-lift
installation of the same engine, which is what the rival built, has that dry thrust and nothing else to
hover on. So the shaft-driven arrangement multiplies the available vertical thrust by

$$\frac{41{,}900}{25{,}000} = 1.676$$

**and it does so without burning any more fuel.** The engine is producing the same power either way.

### An Unpublished Number Recovered From Three Published Ones

**The square-root law says where that factor came from, and it can be inverted to say something the manufacturer never released.**
If the augmentation is entirely the mass-flow effect, then

$$\frac{T_{\text{total}}}{T_{\text{dry}}} = \sqrt{\frac{\dot{m}_{\text{fan}} + \dot{m}_{\text{core}}}{\dot{m}_{\text{core}}}}$$

and solving for the core mass flow, which the engine's manufacturer has never published,

$$\dot{m}_{\text{core}} = \frac{\dot{m}_{\text{fan}}}{r^{2} - 1} = \frac{579.2}{1.676^{2} - 1} = 320.2 \ \text{lb/s}$$

**The open literature's estimate for that engine's airflow is about 270 pounds per second.** The inversion
lands 1.186 times high, which is to say within a fifth,
**from three numbers about thrust and one about a fan, none of which has anything to do with engine airflow.**

**That agreement should be read for what it is and not for more.** The relation assumes the total power is
unchanged between the two arrangements, that both jets are ideal, and that the roll posts belong in the
numerator, and each of those is approximately rather than exactly true. A model with those concessions
landing within twenty percent has demonstrated that the mass-flow mechanism is the dominant one, which is
worth knowing, and it has not measured the engine.

### The Identity the Article Was Already Printing

**The previous article noticed that momentum theory hands you a second quantity for free, and the same thing is true here.**
The disc loading is thrust over disc area,

$$\frac{T}{A} = \frac{88{,}964}{1.2668} = 70.2 \ \text{kPa}$$

and the dynamic pressure in the fully developed jet is

$$q_{\text{jet}} = \tfrac{1}{2} \rho \left(2 v_i\right)^{2} = 2 \rho v_i^{2} = \frac{T}{A}$$

**so the dynamic pressure the jet puts on the ground IS the disc loading, exactly.** The two routes agree to
the last bit of double precision, which is to say the residual is rounding rather than disagreement, and the
identity was confirmed over twenty thousand randomised combinations of thrust, area and density.

This matters because it converts a propulsion number into a facilities number without any further modelling.
**A fifty-inch fan making twenty thousand pounds force is also a machine that presses on whatever it is standing over at 70.2 kilopascals**,
which is about ten pounds per square inch.

### Why Cold Matters More Than the Thrust Does

The core stream is a different animal. Its footprint pressure needs the nozzle exit area, which is not
published, so it is bracketed rather than asserted. Taking the implied core mass flow and a dry military
exit velocity between 550 and 650 metres per second at roughly nine hundred kelvin,

| Assumed exit velocity, m/s | Implied exit area, m² | Footprint pressure, kPa | Ratio to the fan |
|---|---|---|---|
| 550 | 0.673 | 118.9 | 1.69 |
| 600 | 0.617 | 129.7 | 1.85 |
| 650 | 0.570 | 140.5 | 2.00 |

**Across the bracket the core jet presses between 1.69 and 2.00 times as hard as the fan does, and it does so at roughly three times the absolute temperature.**
The fan's efflux leaves at ambient temperature plus the 46.8 kelvin the compression adds. The core's leaves
at something near nine hundred kelvin.

**So the fan's contribution to the design is not only thrust. It is a large volume of cold air placed under the front of the aeroplane**,
which does two things a hotter, faster jet cannot. It reduces the pressure and temperature the landing
surface sees, and it puts a barrier of ambient-temperature air between the hot core efflux and the inlet.
**The previous article treated hot gas ingestion as the rival's central difficulty. This is the architecture that attacks it at the source.**

### The Torque Nobody Mentions

The fan is described everywhere as two-stage counter-rotating, and the phrase is usually read as a
refinement. **It is not a refinement. It is what makes the aircraft controllable.**

A single-rotation fan absorbing shaft power $P$ at angular velocity $\omega$ applies a reaction torque to
the airframe of

$$Q = \frac{P}{\omega}$$

and in a hover there is nothing to react it against except the roll posts, which exist to control the
aircraft rather than to trim it. The roll posts supply a couple of

$$C = 2 F_{\text{post}} \ell$$

where $\ell$ is the distance from the centreline.
**The fan's rotational speed is not published, so the relation is inverted rather than evaluated.** Asking
what speed would make the reaction torque exactly consume the entire roll-post couple gives

| Roll-post arm, m | Roll-post couple, N·m | Threshold speed, rpm |
|---|---|---|
| 2.5 | 43,370 | 4,761 |
| 3.0 | 52,044 | 3,968 |
| 3.5 | 60,718 | 3,401 |
| 4.0 | 69,392 | 2,976 |

**Every threshold in that table is an ordinary fan speed.** An independent estimate of the fan's actual
speed can be built from quantities already computed. The fan raises total pressure by the jet's dynamic
head, giving a pressure ratio of

$$\Pi = \frac{p_0 + q_{\text{jet}}}{p_0} = \frac{101{,}325 + 70{,}229}{101{,}325} = 1.693$$

which for an isentropic compression implies a total temperature rise of 46.8 kelvin, and at a stage loading
coefficient of 0.40 shared between two stages that implies a blade speed near 242 metres per second and a
rotational speed near 3,645 revolutions per minute.

**That estimate sits inside the threshold band and near its middle.** The honest statement is therefore not
that counter-rotation saved a specific percentage, but that
**across every plausible roll-post location a single-rotation fan of this power would have consumed somewhere between three quarters and all of the aircraft's roll authority merely to stand still.**
Counter-rotation does not improve the control system. It is the reason there is one.

### The Clutch, and an Identity That Holds However Gently It Is Engaged

The fan is not always running. In conventional flight it is stopped, its doors are closed, and it is carried
as dead weight. Entering the hovering mode means engaging a clutch between a running engine and a stationary
fan.
**This is the event the article's thesis says was the hard one, so it is worth being exact about what it costs.**

Consider a source held at a constant angular velocity $\omega_s$ driving an inertia $I$ initially at rest,
through a slipping clutch transmitting a torque $Q$ that may vary however it likes. The source does work at
a rate $Q \omega_s$. The inertia receives work at a rate $Q \omega$.
**The difference is destroyed in the clutch.** Over the whole engagement the impulse fixes the total,

$$\int Q \, dt = I \omega_s \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad W_{\text{in}} = \omega_s \int Q \, dt = I \omega_s^{2}$$

while the inertia ends up holding

$$E_{\text{fan}} = \tfrac{1}{2} I \omega_s^{2}$$

so the energy destroyed is the difference,

$$E_{\text{clutch}} = I \omega_s^{2} - \tfrac{1}{2} I \omega_s^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2} I \omega_s^{2}$$

**Exactly half of the energy drawn from the engine during the engagement is destroyed as heat in the clutch, and nothing about that fraction depends on how the engagement is managed.**
A slow, gentle engagement destroys exactly as much as a violent one. The claim was verified independently by
integrating the equations of motion under a constant torque, a linearly rising torque and an exponentially
decaying torque, and the dissipated fraction came back as 0.5 in all three cases.

**The magnitude needs the fan's polar moment of inertia, which is not published, so it is bracketed.**

| Assumed inertia, kg·m² | Fan kinetic energy, MJ | Clutch dissipation, MJ | Stored energy as a time, s |
|---|---|---|---|
| 25 | 1.82 | 1.82 | 0.084 |
| 37 | 2.70 | 2.70 | 0.125 |
| 50 | 3.64 | 3.64 | 0.168 |

**The last column is the useful one and it needs no apology for the bracket.** It is the fan's stored
kinetic energy divided by the power the fan absorbs when running, which is a time, and across the whole
bracket it is under a fifth of a second.
**The fan stores less than a fifth of a second of its own operating power.**

### What the Bound Rules Out

The clutch is quoted as engaging and disengaging in under nine seconds.
**Combining that with the rated shaft power gives a bound that assumes nothing at all about the fan.** At
most the rated power can flow for at most the quoted time, and at most half of it can be destroyed, so

$$E_{\text{clutch}} \le \tfrac{1}{2} P t = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 21.63 \times 10^{6} \times 9 = 97.3 \ \text{MJ}$$

**That bound is absurd and its absurdity is the finding.** Ninety-seven megajoules deposited into an assumed
twenty kilograms of carbon would raise its temperature by about 6,853 kelvin, which is beyond the
vaporisation point of anything. The engagement therefore cannot be anywhere near power-limited.

**Comparing the bound with the bracket says by how much.** Spreading the real dissipation over the quoted
nine seconds gives a mean power between 1.9 and 3.7 percent of what the shaft could deliver.
**The nine seconds is not the time the energy requires. It is the time the heat requires**, and the
difference between those two statements is the whole reason a mode change on this aircraft is a deliberate,
scheduled event rather than the flick of a switch.

## The Vehicle

Two airframes covered three configurations. The X-35A flew as a conventional fighter from 24 October 2000,
was then rebuilt with the lift system installed, and flew again as the X-35B. The X-35C was a separate
aircraft carrying the carrier variant's larger wing and heavier structure.

The demonstrators were [deliberately simpler than the production aircraft][ref_codeone]. They carried no
weapons bays, no radar, no mission systems and no low-observable treatment of the kind the product would
need, and they used off-the-shelf components wherever schedule allowed.
**The published empty weight of 26,500 pounds and maximum takeoff weight of fifty thousand pounds belong to a machine built to answer a question, not to fight.**

## Dependent Systems

### The Three-Bearing Swivel Module

The rear nozzle redirects the core exhaust downward through a jointed pipe whose three canted bearings,
rotated relative to one another, sweep the nozzle through ninety-five degrees in 2.5 seconds.
**The elegance is that a purely rotational mechanism produces a large angular deflection**, so the sealing
problem is a set of rotating joints rather than a set of sliding ones, at a station carrying the full core
efflux.

### The Inlet

The inlet is a [diverterless supersonic design][ref_dsi], replacing the boundary-layer diverter of a
conventional installation with a fixed compression surface that pushes the boundary layer sideways.
**It removes weight, moving parts and radar return at once**, and it does so at the cost of being optimised
for one region of the envelope rather than adjustable across it. For a demonstrator cleared to about Mach
1.1 that cost is invisible, which is worth remembering when reading the supersonic leg of Mission X.

### Roll Posts and Control Power

Bleed from the engine's fan is ducted to nozzles in each wing, giving 1,950 pounds force each.
**In a hover an aeroplane has no aerodynamic control at all**, so every axis must be held by thrust
modulation. Pitch comes from splitting thrust between the lift fan and the rear nozzle, yaw from vectoring
the rear nozzle laterally, and roll from the posts. The earlier finding about counter-rotation is the reason
the posts are sized for control rather than for trim.

### Structure and the Variant Problem

The three variants share a fuselage cross-section and a great deal of structure, and differ in wing area, in
landing gear, and in whether a lift fan occupies the volume immediately behind the cockpit.
**That shared volume is the hardest constraint in the whole design**, because the conventional and carrier
variants carry fuel where the STOVL variant carries a fan, and the airframe has to be the same airframe for
the commonality argument to pay.

## The Flight Test Record

### The Precedents, Because One of Them Matters More Than Is Usually Said

**Two aircraft had already solved parts of this problem.** The [Harrier][ref_harrier] made vertical landing
an operational reality from the late 1960s using a single engine with four rotating nozzles, and it was
never supersonic. The Yak-141 was supersonic and hovered, using two dedicated lift engines and a main engine
exhausting through a **three-bearing swivel nozzle**.

**That last phrase should stop a reader, because it is the X-35's rear nozzle.** Lockheed and Yakovlev
entered a commercial agreement in the early 1990s under which Lockheed provided funding in exchange for
design data, and the resemblance between the two swivel modules is close and widely noted.
**How much of the X-35's nozzle descends from that arrangement is disputed and this article does not attempt to settle it**,
but the concept was not invented at Palmdale and the article would be misleading if it implied otherwise.
**The shaft-driven lift fan is the genuinely new idea. The nozzle behind it has a longer history.**

### What Actually Flew

| Aircraft | First flight | Flights | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| X-35A | 24 October 2000 | 27 in 30 days | Conventional, completed 22 November 2000 |
| X-35C | 16 December 2000 | 73, 58 hours | Carrier variant, completed 11 March 2001 |
| X-35B | 23 June 2001, first vertical | 23 June to 30 July 2001 | Rebuilt from the X-35A |

The X-35B's totals across its short campaign were 27 vertical landings, 14 short takeoffs, 18 vertical
takeoffs, five supersonic flights and five aerial refuellings.

**One number in the table is disputed and the disagreement is worth recording rather than resolving.**
Contemporary programme reporting gives the X-35A 27 flights in thirty days, while some later reference
accounts give 28. Nothing in this article turns on which is right.

### The Eleven Days That Contain the Answer

**This is the section the article exists for.** Setting the X-35B's flights out in order, with the first
occurrence of each capability marked, does something no summary of Mission X does.

| Date, 2001 | Event | First of its kind for this aircraft |
|---|---|---|
| 23 June | Vertical takeoff, hover, vertical landing at Palmdale | Yes |
| 24 June | First sustained hover | Yes |
| late June | Seventeen vertical takeoffs, hovers and landings completed | No |
| 9 July | [In-flight conversion to hovering mode, aerial refuelling, and Mach 1.08, in one sortie][ref_lm_conversion] | **Yes, and this is the hard one** |
| 16 July | [Short takeoff, wingborne to jet-borne transition, vertical landing][ref_lm_shorttakeoff] | Short takeoff, yes |
| 20 July | **Mission X**, short takeoff, Mach 1.05, vertical landing | **No. Nothing on this sortie was new** |
| 26 July | Mission X repeated at over 34,000 pounds | No |
| 30 July | [Campaign complete][ref_lm_completion] | |

**By 16 July the aircraft had already flown every element of Mission X.** It had converted between modes in
flight, it had gone supersonic, it had taken off short, it had transitioned from wingborne to jet-borne
flight, and it had landed vertically. The programme manager said so at the time, in those terms, four days
before the famous flight.

**And the 9 July sortie went faster than Mission X did.** It reached Mach 1.08 against Mission X's Mach
1.05, and it did so on the same flight as the aircraft's first in-flight conversion to hovering mode and an
aerial refuelling.

**So Mission X contained no manoeuvre the aircraft had not already performed, and it was not the aircraft's fastest flight.**
What it contained was the assembly. That is a real thing to have demonstrated, and it is a different thing
from what the reputation implies.

## Comparison With Ground Prediction

### The Short Takeoff, Reconstructed

The 26 July repetition is documented well enough to be rebuilt. The aircraft weighed over 34,000 pounds,
used approximately five hundred feet of runway, and left the ground at about sixty knots. The 20 July flight
left the ground at about eighty knots.

**At unstick the weight is carried by two things, and only two.** Writing $L$ for wing lift, $T_v$ for
whatever the lift system points downward and $W$ for weight,

$$W = L + T_v = \tfrac{1}{2} \rho V^{2} S C_L + T_v$$

With the rear nozzle pointing aft, the fixed vertical contribution is the fan and the roll posts alone,

$$T_v = 20{,}000 + 2 \times 1{,}950 = 23{,}900 \ \text{lbf}$$

**That fixed vertical contribution is 23,900 pounds force, which is 70.3 percent of the aircraft's weight.**
The wing therefore has to find only the remaining 10,100 pounds force, and at eighty knots over 41.81 square
metres of wing that requires

$$C_L = \frac{10{,}100 \times 4.448}{\tfrac{1}{2} \times 1.225 \times 41.16^{2} \times 41.81} = 1.036$$

**A lift coefficient of 1.036 at unstick is unremarkable for a fighter wing at a moderate angle of attack, and that is the point.**
The eighty-knot unstick is fully explained by the fan carrying seven tenths of the aeroplane and the wing
carrying three tenths at an ordinary lift coefficient. The number was independently recovered by bisecting
on speed at the stated coefficient rather than by solving for the coefficient at the stated speed.

**The sixty-knot takeoff then follows without any new assumption.** At sixty knots the same wing at the same
coefficient supplies only 5,681 pounds force, so the rear nozzle must be deflected to make up the
difference, and the angle required is

$$\theta = \arcsin\!\left(\frac{34{,}000 - 23{,}900 - 5{,}681}{18{,}000}\right) = 14.21^{\circ}$$

**The two takeoffs differ by about fourteen degrees of nozzle.** That is the entire difference between the
eighty-knot and the sixty-knot cases, and it is a small deliberate movement of one control.

### The Ground Roll, Which Does Not Close Without an Admission

Running the same configuration forward through the ground roll is where a discrepancy appears. With the
nozzle at 14.21 degrees the horizontal component is 17,449 pounds force, and time-stepping the equation of
motion with speed-dependent drag and rolling friction on the unloaded wheels reaches sixty knots in

$$s_{\min} = 314.9 \ \text{ft}$$

**against a quoted five hundred.** The quoted roll is 1.588 times the minimum, which corresponds to an
achieved acceleration of 0.3187 times gravity against an available 0.506.

**The gap is real and it is not an error in the reconstruction.** Only about 63 percent of the available
horizontal thrust appears in the quoted distance. Thrust build-up from brake release accounts for part of
it, and a progressive rather than instantaneous nozzle movement accounts for more.

**But the honest reading of the gap is the interesting one, and it is the second finding of this section.**
Acceleration was not scarce. An aircraft that can reach its unstick speed in 315 feet and takes 500 is not
straining, and there is no reason it should have been strained, because of the number in the next paragraph.

### The Takeoff Did Not Have to Be Short

**Total vertical thrust is 41,900 pounds force and the aircraft weighed 34,000 pounds.**

$$\frac{T_{\text{total}}}{W} = \frac{41{,}900}{34{,}000} = 1.232$$

**At the weight it flew Mission X, the X-35B could have taken off vertically.** It had done so eighteen
times. The vertical landing weight limit, meaning the weight at which vertical thrust exactly equals weight,
is 41,900 pounds, and the aircraft was nearly eight thousand pounds below it at the start of the sortie.

**So the short takeoff in Mission X was a demonstration of a technique rather than the relief of a constraint.**
A short takeoff exists in the operational requirement because the aeroplane that matters will be heavier
than its vertical thrust, and will need wing lift to get airborne with a useful load. The demonstrator was
not in that condition on 20 July, and neither the flight nor the arithmetic claims it was.

### The Supersonic Leg Was Thermally Free

Mission X reached Mach 1.05 at twenty-five thousand feet. The standard atmosphere there gives a static
temperature of 238.62 kelvin, a density of 0.5489 kilograms per cubic metre and a speed of sound of 309.7
metres per second, so the aircraft was travelling at 325.2 metres per second. The stagnation temperature
follows from the energy equation,

$$T_0 = T + \frac{V^{2}}{2 c_p} = 238.62 + \frac{325.2^{2}}{2 \times 1004.7} = 291.2 \ \text{K}$$

**which is 18.1 degrees Celsius.** The hottest air the airframe met during its supersonic dash was 3.1
kelvin warmer than a standard day at sea level.

**There was no thermal event.** Kinetic heating at low supersonic speed is negligible, and any argument that
sequencing a supersonic dash before a vertical landing subjected the lift system to a hot start has nothing
to stand on. The atmosphere was reached here by numerically integrating the hydrostatic equation rather than
by evaluating the barometric power law, and the stagnation temperature through the energy equation rather
than the Mach-number form.

Nor was thrust scarce. At that condition the dynamic pressure is 29,018 pascals, an estimated transonic drag
coefficient of 0.035 gives about 9,546 pounds force of drag, and the augmented engine at that density still
offers roughly 22,805 pounds force, a ratio of

$$\frac{T}{D} = 2.389$$

**The aircraft was not working to hold Mach 1.05.** It was flying at an envelope limit set by the test
programme, on a demonstrator whose inlet and structure had been cleared to a little over Mach 1.1, and the
previous sortie had already reached Mach 1.08.

### The Vertical Landing Was the Easiest of the Three

**The vertical landing came last, which means it came at the lowest weight of the day.** Every pound of fuel
burned during the climb, the dash and the recovery is a pound the lift system does not have to hold up.

Taking a sortie fuel burn of 3,500 pounds, which is an assumption and is labelled as one, the landing weight
is 30,500 pounds and the margin becomes

$$\frac{41{,}900}{30{,}500} = 1.374$$

**against 1.232 at takeoff, a gain of 1.115 from the ordering alone.**

**The three events were flown in the order that makes each of them easiest.** The short takeoff came first,
when the aircraft was heaviest and a rolling start was most useful. The supersonic dash came in the middle,
where it burned the fuel. The vertical landing came last, when the aircraft was lightest and the manoeuvre
most comfortable.
**An operational sortie would be flown in exactly that order, so this is not a criticism of the profile. It is an observation that the profile does not test a worst case, and it was never claimed to.**

The worst case for this architecture is a vertical landing at high weight with stores still aboard, which is
the bring-back problem the previous article examined in detail for the rival.
**Mission X did not go near it.**

## What the Data Changed

### The Answer

**Mission X was evidence for one proposition and display for another, and the two are easy to conflate.**

It is genuine evidence that the installation requires no reconfiguration between hovering and supersonic
flight. That is a real architectural property, the rival did not have it, and a single sortie moving through
both regimes demonstrates it as directly as anything could.

**It is not evidence that the combination itself was new, and a claim often made for Mission X is simply wrong.**
The [Yakovlev Yak-141][ref_yak141] flew supersonically in 1987 and completed full transitions from 1990, so
a vertical-landing aircraft capable of supersonic flight without reconfiguration existed more than a decade
earlier. **What was new on 20 July 2001 was the sequence in one sortie, not the capability.**

**It is not evidence that any of the three regimes was individually difficult for this aircraft, because the arithmetic says none of them was.**
The short takeoff was flown by an aeroplane that could have gone straight up. The supersonic dash raised the
stagnation temperature by three kelvin over a sea-level standard day and used 41.9 percent of the thrust
available. The vertical landing happened at the lightest the aircraft had been all day.

**And the sortie was not where the engineering risk was retired.** Every element had been flown already, the
first in-flight conversion had happened on 9 July, and that sortie went faster.
**The information was retired on 9 July and the demonstration was performed on 20 July.**

**That is not a criticism of anyone.** A demonstration exists to make something legible to people who will
not read a flight test report, and Mission X did that better than any report could.
**But a flight that transfers no new information to the engineers and a great deal to everyone else is a display, and calling it by its name costs the programme nothing.**

### What the Programme Settled

The programme established that a shaft-driven lift fan works on an aeroplane, which had never been shown at
this scale or this power, and the team received the [Collier Trophy][ref_collier] for 2001 on that basis. It
established that the clutch, gearbox and drive shaft survive repeated engagement in flight. It established
that mode conversion can be flown as a routine event rather than as a test point.
**And it established, by the counter-rotation argument above, that a fan of this power can be installed without consuming the aircraft's roll authority.**

### What It Fed Into

The architecture went into production essentially unchanged in principle, which is unusual. The production
lift system kept the shaft drive, the counter-rotating fan, the clutch, the three-bearing swivel module and
the roll posts.

**The literature followed the aircraft rather than the designation, and this is the mirror image of the previous two articles' finding.**
The X-33 and the X-34 each stopped generating literature under their own names the moment they were
cancelled, and this article's subject shows the control case.
**The X-35 cluster is also thin, and for the opposite reason. The work did not stop. It changed name.**

### What It Failed to Influence

**The demonstration did not settle the weight question, and the weight question is what nearly ended the production programme.**
The STOVL variant's weight growth during development forced a major redesign several years later, and
nothing in the 2001 campaign predicted it or could have.
**A demonstrator that weighs 34,000 pounds tells you very little about an aeroplane that will weigh far more**,
and the architecture's thrust margin is precisely the quantity that weight growth attacks.

## Where the Framing Breaks Down

### The Deflationary Reading Can Be Pushed Too Far

**The argument above is capable of proving too much.** If one insists that a demonstration teaching the
engineers nothing new is theatre, then almost every public demonstration in aviation history is theatre,
which is a sign the criterion is wrong rather than a discovery about aviation.

**A demonstration has a second, legitimate function, which is to establish that separately verified capabilities compose.**
Engineers frequently find that they do not. Doing the three in sequence tests the aircraft's ability to do
them in sequence, including the fuel state, the thermal state, the pilot's workload and the systems'
behaviour after a long, busy sortie.
**None of those is captured by the arithmetic in this article, and all of them are real.**

### Mach 1.05 Is the Worst Place on the Drag Curve, Not the Easiest

**The claim that the supersonic leg was cheap deserves its strongest counter-argument stated properly.**
Transonic drag rises steeply and peaks a little above Mach one, so Mach 1.05 is close to the most expensive
point on the whole drag curve rather than a comfortable cruise. An aircraft that reaches Mach 1.05 in level
flight has demonstrated that it can push through the peak, which is a stiffer test than reaching a higher
Mach number would be once past it.

**That counter-argument is correct on drag and does not disturb the thermal conclusion**, which is separate
and which the arithmetic settles. It also does not disturb the ordering conclusion.
**A conclusion that survives its own best counter-argument is worth more than one that needed the argument suppressed.**

### The Assumed Inputs and What They Carry

Several results here rest on quantities nobody published, and it is worth being explicit about which
conclusions would move if the assumptions moved.

| Assumed quantity | Used for | Does the conclusion depend on it? |
|---|---|---|
| Core mass flow of 270 lb/s, from the open literature | Comparing against the inverted 320.2 | No. The inversion is the result; the comparison is a check |
| Fan polar moment of inertia, 25 to 50 kg·m² | Clutch energy magnitude | No. The halving identity is exact and the time constant is under a fifth of a second across the bracket |
| Stage loading coefficient of 0.40 | Estimating fan speed | Weakly. Every threshold in the counter-rotation table is an ordinary fan speed regardless |
| Roll-post arm, 2.5 to 4.0 m | Counter-rotation threshold | No. The conclusion is stated across the whole bracket |
| Zero-lift drag 0.025, rolling friction 0.03 | Ground roll | Slightly. The gap between 315 and 500 feet is far larger than these move it |
| Transonic drag coefficient 0.035 | Dash thrust margin | No. The margin is 2.389 and would survive a doubling |
| Sortie fuel burn of 3,500 lb | Landing weight margin | Yes, and the assumption-free statement is given beside it, being a weight limit of 41,900 pounds |

### A Demonstration Is Not Only an Experiment

**The framing this whole series uses treats a research aircraft as an instrument for answering a question, and the X-35 does not fit that framing cleanly.**
It was a competitor as much as an instrument. Its purpose included persuading a customer, and a machine
built partly to persuade is not well described by asking only what it measured.
**The framing does not break down so much as become incomplete**, and the incompleteness is exactly the
space in which Mission X sits.

## The Contemporary Literature

The standing directive for this series asks each article to serve as a survey of the current literature as
well as a study of its aircraft.
**For this subject the survey is unusually rewarding, because almost every question the X-35 raised is being asked again right now by people building something else entirely.**

### Powered Lift Moved to Electric Aircraft and Took the Physics With It

**The single largest change since 2001 is that the momentum theory in this article stopped being a military speciality.**
Disc loading, figure of merit, hover efficiency and outwash are now the working vocabulary of electric
vertical-takeoff aircraft, and the literature has grown by orders of magnitude in the last decade.

**The relation is identical and the answer comes out the other way.** Thrust per unit power is inversely
proportional to jet velocity, so a designer free to choose disc area will choose a large one. The X-35's fan
sits at 70.2 kilopascals of disc loading because it had to fit inside a supersonic fighter. An electric
aircraft with no such constraint runs one or two orders of magnitude lower and buys enormous hover
efficiency for it.
**The X-35 is the extreme high-disc-loading end of exactly the trade the current literature explores at the other end.**

### The Lift Fan Itself

**The shaft-driven lift fan remains a nearly unique artefact and its literature is correspondingly small.**
What has grown instead is the turbomachinery beneath it. Counter-rotating stages, which the X-35 adopted for
the torque reason set out earlier, are now studied for their own aerodynamic merits, and the modern work on
stage matching and on hollow blade construction is where a reader should go for the fan itself rather than
to anything carrying the aircraft's name.

### Nozzles, Inlets and Installed Performance

**Thrust vectoring outlived the specific application.** The swivelling nozzle is now studied mostly for
attitude control on launch vehicles and for manoeuvre enhancement on fighters, and the diverterless inlet
became a standard feature rather than an experiment.
**Installed performance accounting, which is where the thrust lapse in this article's dash calculation properly belongs, remains the least glamorous and most consequential part of the subject.**

### Performance, Weight and the Programme

**Weight growth is the subject this article's aircraft failed to illuminate and the literature has since taken seriously.**
The contemporary work treats mass properties as a programme risk to be forecast and tracked rather than as
an outcome, which is precisely the lesson the production programme learned expensively after the
demonstrator had answered every question it was asked.

### Method, Uncertainty and Computation

**The methodological change since 2001 is larger than any single technical one.** Uncertainty
quantification, surrogate modelling and machine learning now sit between the wind tunnel and the design, and
a reconstruction of the kind this article performs by hand would today be posed as an inference problem with
stated priors.
**That is better practice and it is worth saying that it would not have changed any conclusion here**,
because the quantities that mattered were bracketed rather than estimated.

## The Source Base

### Both Halves, Counted and Not Only Divided

**The count and the fraction are reported together, because they move independently and reporting only the fraction misrepresents both.**
Adding contemporary sources leaves the period count untouched while lowering its share, and adding period
sources does the same to the contemporary share. Neither movement is a fact about coverage.

The article cites 2,820 records published through 2001, the year the competition was decided, and 2,514
published from 2015 onward.

### A Designation That Generated No Literature At All

**This is the sharpest thing the source base contains, and it was not anticipated.**

The pool assembled for this article holds 7,567 harvested records.
**Not one of them carries "X-35" in its title.** Three separate harvests asked for it directly, including
queries reading "X-35 flight test results", "X-35B STOVL flight demonstration" and "X-35C carrier variant
flight test". The result was zero, every time.

**The previous two articles found something that looked similar and means the opposite.** The X-33's cluster
held sixty records and every one predated 2002. The X-34's held its records and every one predated 2002.
Both programmes were cancelled, and the conclusion drawn was that a cancelled programme stops generating
literature under its own name, so the documentary trace of a vehicle measures how long it survived rather
than what it contributed.

**The X-35 is the control case for that claim and it fails it in an unexpected direction.** This programme
was not cancelled. It won, and its architecture went into production and is flying now.
**And its designation has a smaller documentary trace than either of the cancelled vehicles, because it never had one.**

What the literature carries instead is the programme name and the product name. Forty records name the Joint
Strike Fighter, running from 1996 to 2022. Twelve name the F-35, running from 2003 to 2020.
**Nothing names the aeroplane.**

**The inference this supports is narrower than it first appears, and it is worth stating carefully.** The
X-35 designation was applied to competition demonstrators built by a contractor and flown for a source
selection, and that is not the institutional arrangement that produces published reports. The X-33 and the
X-34 were agency programmes with agency reporting obligations, which is why their cancelled programmes still
left a paper trail.
**So the finding is about who was writing rather than about who won, and the three cases together say that the documentary trace measures the institution rather than the aircraft.**
That belongs in the closing article.

### Which Subjects Are Thin, and Which of the Three Kinds

**Seven subjects remain thin after three harvests aimed at them, and they are not all thin for the same reason.**
A331 established that a subject can be thin because the work was never done, because the heading is wrong,
or because the knowledge is so settled that it stopped generating papers.

| Subject | Records | Which kind of thin |
|---|---|---|
| Ground roll and takeoff distance | 1 | **Settled.** A closed-form result in every performance textbook |
| Standard atmosphere | 9, none modern | **Settled.** A standards document, not a research literature |
| Disc loading | 3 | **Wrong heading.** The subject sits inside the momentum theory cluster, which holds 164 |
| Jet footprint and ground erosion | 4 | **Wrong heading.** It lives inside impingement and ground environment work |
| Stagnation temperature and kinetic heating | 14, one modern | **Moved.** The modern half of this subject is hypersonics and left the transonic case behind |
| Thrust lapse with altitude | 12, two modern | **Wrong heading.** It lives inside installed performance and engine decks |
| Rotor spin-up and inertia | 7 | **Wrong heading.** It lives inside drive system transient work |

**None of these is padded and none is reported as a gap in the field.** Six of the seven are headings rather
than subjects, and the article cites the literature where it actually lives.

The following books and monographs were drawn on for the standing theory rather than for the aircraft,
covering propulsion, powered lift, rotor and fan aerodynamics, aircraft performance and flight test method.
**Almost none of them is about the X-35 and that is the point**, since the relations this article displays
are older than the aeroplane and better documented than it.

### What Counts as Primary Here

Primary for this subject means the reports and papers written during the competition and the technology work
that preceded it, together with the contemporary programme announcements that record what was flown and
when. **The flight chronology in this article rests on the latter**, because the demonstrator campaign was a
contractor activity and its detailed test reports are not public.

### What the Record Does Not Contain

There is no published flight test report for the X-35B, and the standard survey of the
[American X-vehicles][ref_xvehicles] treats the type in a page. There is no published weight statement, no
published engine deck, no published fan map, and no published moment of inertia for the lift fan.
**The quantitative reconstruction in this article is built entirely from performance figures released for publicity and from the physics that connects them**,
and the article says so at every point where an assumption was needed.

## Epistemic State

### Historical Fact

The X-35A first flew on 24 October 2000 and completed its conventional campaign on 22 November 2000. The
X-35C first flew on 16 December 2000 and completed 73 flights and 58 hours by 11 March 2001. The X-35A was
rebuilt as the X-35B, which made its first vertical takeoff and landing on 23 June 2001 and completed
testing on 30 July 2001. On 9 July 2001 it performed its first in-flight conversion to hovering mode,
refuelled in the air, and reached Mach 1.08 on the same sortie. On 16 July 2001 it flew a short takeoff, a
transition and a vertical landing. On 20 July 2001 Major Art Tomassetti flew Mission X, and on 26 July 2001
Simon Hargreaves repeated it at a weight over 34,000 pounds. The contract was awarded to Lockheed Martin on
26 October 2001. The lift system's published figures are a fifty-inch two-stage counter-rotating fan
producing twenty thousand pounds force from twenty-nine thousand shaft horsepower, a three-bearing swivel
module passing eighteen thousand pounds force and rotating ninety-five degrees in 2.5 seconds, and roll
posts of 1,950 pounds force each.

### Engineering Analysis

The fan's figure of merit of 0.697, its induced velocity of 169.3 metres per second, its mass flow of 579.2
pounds per second and its disc loading of 70.2 kilopascals follow from published geometry and performance by
momentum theory. The augmentation ratio of 1.676 and the implied core mass flow of 320.2 pounds per second
follow from the square-root law. The identity that a hovering jet's dynamic pressure equals its disc loading
is exact. The identity that exactly half the energy drawn through a clutch engaging a stationary inertia is
destroyed is exact and independent of the torque profile. The stagnation temperature of 291.2 kelvin at Mach
1.05 and twenty-five thousand feet follows from the standard atmosphere and the energy equation. The unstick
lift coefficient of 1.036, the nozzle deflection of 14.21 degrees and the minimum ground roll of 314.9 feet
follow from the lift and momentum balances.
**All fifty-one checks were reproduced by an independent verifier that does not import the calculation, using bisection, numerical integration, time-stepping and randomised property tests.**

### Inference

That Mission X was the assembly of already-demonstrated elements rather than the retirement of technical
risk is an inference from the flight chronology, and it is a strong one, because the programme's own
contemporary statements list every element as already flown four days earlier. That the genuinely novel
event was the in-flight conversion of 9 July is an inference of the same kind. That counter-rotation was
necessary rather than merely desirable is an inference from an inverted threshold calculation across a
bracket of assumed roll-post positions. That the short takeoff was a technique demonstration rather than a
necessity follows from the thrust margin of 1.232 and is close to a deduction.

### What the Record Does Not Settle

**Whether the fly-off would have gone the other way without Mission X is not settled and cannot be.** Source
selection weighs many things, the flight was three months before the decision, and no public document
apportions the decision among its inputs.

**Whether the X-32 could have flown an equivalent profile with more development time is not settled.** Its
architecture required reconfiguration as built, but the question of whether that was fundamental or
contingent is a design question that was never taken far enough to answer.

**The magnitudes of the clutch energies are not settled**, because the fan's moment of inertia has never
been published. The halving identity is exact and the bracket is wide, and the article reports both.

**Whether the demonstration's persuasive function should count as part of its engineering value is a question of judgement rather than fact**,
and this article deliberately answers it in two directions in two different sections.

## Out of Scope

The production F-35 programme, its cost and schedule history, and the 2004 weight reduction effort are
outside this article, which is about a demonstrator that flew in 2001. The low-observable design of either
competitor is outside it. The avionics and sensor fusion that dominate the production aircraft's reputation
are outside it, because the demonstrators carried none. The carrier variant's approach and arrestment
characteristics are touched on only where they bear on the variant weight argument. The source selection
process itself, and the construct-validity argument about demonstrators generally, are covered in the
article on the X-32 and are not repeated here.

## Conclusion

**The X-35 answered the question of whether a supersonic fighter can hover without being rebuilt between the two, and the answer is yes, by carrying a fan it does not use most of the time.**

The fan is worth carrying because thrust rises as the square root of mass flow at fixed power, so moving air
the engine never touched multiplies vertical thrust by 1.676 without burning more fuel. It is
counter-rotating because a single-rotation fan of that power would have consumed most or all of the
aircraft's roll authority merely to stand still. Its exhaust is cold because the landing surface and the
inlet both care more about temperature and pressure than about thrust, and a fan presses about half as hard
as the core does at a third of the temperature.

**Mission X, the flight the aircraft is remembered for, was not where any of that was established.** Every
element of it had been flown before 20 July 2001, the first in-flight conversion had happened eleven days
earlier on a sortie that went faster, and the arithmetic shows that none of the three events was
individually demanding for an aircraft with 41,900 pounds force of vertical thrust and a weight of 34,000.
The short takeoff was flown by an aeroplane that could have gone straight up. The supersonic dash raised the
stagnation temperature 3.1 kelvin above a standard sea-level day. The vertical landing happened at the
lightest weight of the sortie, in the ordering that makes it easiest.

**The sortie was a demonstration in the exact sense of the word, and that is not a criticism.** It made an
architectural property legible in ninety seconds to people who would never read a test report, and it did so
honestly, because the property was real and the rival did not have it.
**What it was not is the experiment.** The experiment was the clutch engaging in flight on 9 July, and
nobody remembers the date.
